CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
This is a 52-year-old male with a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion. The patient presented to his primary care provider, Dr. Henry Howard, on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months. He denied any trouble with headaches in the past. Workup for worsening headaches was initiated with brain MRI and serology where a pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered. The patient describes headaches located behind his eyes as a dull nagging ache with gradual onset approximately three months ago. Initial severity was 3/10 and has progressively worsened to 6/10. Headaches tend to be worse in the morning, last a few hours at a time, and nothing makes them better or worse. He reports recently bumping into door frames. He denies associated nausea, fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or syncope. He reports eyes were checked in the fall with no noted changes. He attempted treatment with Tylenol a few times without improvement. MRI brain with contrast from 3/4/21 reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. The ventricles are normal in size and no other abnormalities are noted.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies nausea, fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or syncope. Reports recent bumping into door frames. Denies subjective vision changes. Denies balance changes.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable.

MEDICATIONS
No regular medications. Tried Tylenol a few times for headaches without relief.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient was adopted and has no knowledge of family history.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years. Recently purchased a small house. Denies alcohol use, tobacco use, and recreational drug use.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Patient is alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate and speech is fluent. Cranial nerve examination is grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity is normal. Eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

RESULTS
Labs dated 3/3/21: CBC, CMP, coagulation studies, and CRP all normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates low TSH with all other results normal. MRI brain with contrast from 3/4/21: well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles are normal in size. No other abnormalities noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diagnosis: Pituitary adenoma, benign appearing. Patient is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression. Surgical intervention with transsphenoidal approach for excision and decompression of the pituitary fossa is indicated. Risks of surgery discussed including anesthesia risks (myocardial infarction, stroke, death) and surgical risks (infection, need for further surgery, cerebrospinal fluid leak, seizure, stroke, permanent neurological deficits including numbness, weakness, and difficulty speaking, and death). Patient to be referred to surgery scheduler for scheduling. Visual field test to be arranged today or tomorrow for pre-operative baseline. Ophthalmology referral for full eye examination and visual field mapping of peripheral vision prior to surgery to allow for post-operative comparison. Pathology will be obtained on removed adenoma to confirm diagnosis.
